title: First 112 workers fly to Malaysia at zero cost as market reopens
excerpt: The government-run BOESL sent 112 workers to Malaysia at no migration cost, the first since recruitment stopped in mid-2024. Another 225 are due to go in December.
content:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday (26 November) saw off the first 112 workers going to Malaysia under a government scheme in which the employer pays all migration costs, bdnews24.com and The Daily Star reported. It is the first group to go since Malaysia stopped hiring Bangladeshi workers in June 2024, after allegations of syndicate recruitment, excessive costs, corruption and exploitation.

The workers were chosen from 4,039 applicants through an open e-lottery and direct interviews by employers, with the process run by the state-owned Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL). According to bdnews24.com, they will work for DHL Supply Chain in Malaysia for 1,700 ringgit a month on renewable three-year contracts, with housing and medical care provided by the employer.

Another 225 workers are due to go in December, and BOESL has received attested demand letters from four Malaysian companies for 1,048 workers. The prime minister said about 10,000 workers could go to Malaysia at almost no cost through the initiative. Speaking at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, he said the government would start teaching workers the languages of destination countries "within the next few months".

The launch came a day after Malaysia's home minister, Saifuddin Nasution Ismail, told the Malaysian parliament in a written answer that Bangladeshis were involved in 6,898 cases of breaching immigration pass conditions between 2023 and 15 September 2026, the most of any nationality, bdnews24.com reported, citing The Star. Most such cases involve people working on social visit passes, which do not allow work.

Why it matters

Malaysia took about 450,000 Bangladeshi workers between 2022 and May 2024, many of whom paid large sums to brokers and some of whom arrived to find no job. A government-to-government route at zero cost could set a benchmark, but 112 workers is a tiny share of demand. Migrant rights groups have warned that most cheated migrants had no written contract, and the 10,000-worker plan announced last week still leaves the wider private recruitment system unchanged.

What to watch

  • Whether the December batch of 225 leaves on time and on the same terms.
  • How private recruiting agencies will be allowed back into the Malaysia market, and at what cost cap.
  • Complaints from the first workers once they start work.
